Areas of Investigation

Research Interests

Combining experimental characterization with micromechanical modeling to understand the behavior of cementitious materials across scales.

My research focuses on the behavior and performance of cementitious materials, with particular attention to low-carbon and blended systems. I combine experimental techniques such as thermogravimetric analysis, micro-indentation, and mechanical testing to characterize hydration, strength, and durability. In parallel, I develop micromechanical models to predict the mechanical properties and evolution of microstructure over time. This multi-scale approach allows for a better understanding of how material composition and curing conditions influence macroscopic properties. The goal is to support the development of sustainable, high-performance concretes through a deeper scientific understanding of their behavior.

🔬

Hydration Kinetics

Calorimetric and TGA analysis of cement hydration phases in blended systems. Tracking C-S-H precipitation, portlandite formation and their modification by SCMs.

From the Laboratory

Investigation Framework

Multiscale Approach

Nano-scale
0.1 – 100 nm
C-S-H nanostructure, gel pore network, calcium silicate chains, interlayer water. SAXS/SANS and molecular-level analysis.
Micro-scale
1 – 100 µm
Cement paste, hydration products, unhydrated clinker, capillary porosity. SEM-BSE and micro-indentation grid mapping.
Meso-scale
0.1 – 10 mm
Mortar matrix, aggregate-paste ITZ, shrinkage cracks, recycled sand inclusion. X-ray µ-CT and DIC analysis.
Macro-scale
10 mm – 1 m
Structural concrete elements, macroscopic mechanical response, durability under environmental exposure. Standard and accelerated testing protocols.
TGA / DSC
Thermogravimetric analysis for quantifying hydration products and bound water content.
Nanoindentation
Mechanical properties (E, H) at the phase level with large-scale statistical grid mapping.
SEM-EDS
Backscattered electron imaging with elemental mapping for phase distribution analysis.
Mechanical Testing
Compressive, flexural and fracture characterization from specimen to structural scale.
XRD / Rietveld
Phase quantification of clinker minerals and hydration products at early and late ages.
MIP / BET
Pore size distribution, specific surface area and total porosity characterization.

Theoretical & Computational Framework

Micromechanical Modeling

Bridging observed microstructure and predicted effective properties through rigorous homogenization theory and phase-mechanics coupling.

Micromechanical models translate phase composition, morphology, and individual phase elastic/creep properties — measured by nanoindentation — into effective macroscopic responses. This bottom-up strategy links nano-scale C-S-H stiffness and packing density to paste, mortar and concrete elastic moduli, creep compliance and shrinkage, providing predictive tools for mixture design optimization with mineral additions.

🔀 View Upscaling Homogenization Workflow Diagram ⌄

Upscaling Homogenization Workflow

01
Phase Input
C-S-H, CH, clinker, SCM properties from nanoindentation
02
RVE Definition
Representative Volume Element at each scale level
03
Homogenization
Mori-Tanaka or Self-Consistent averaging scheme
04
Effective Properties
E, ν, creep J(t), shrinkage ε at paste & concrete scale
05
Validation
Comparison with macroscopic experimental measurements
Elasticity

Mori-Tanaka Scheme

Matrix-inclusion framework for effective elastic stiffness of cement paste. Accounts for inclusion shape, volume fractions and phase moduli from nanoindentation grids.

C_eff = [Σ fᵢ Cᵢ : Aᵢ] : [Σ fᵢ Aᵢ]⁻¹
Elasticity

Self-Consistent Scheme

Iterative approach suited for polycrystalline or interpenetrating microstructures without a dominant matrix phase. Applied to high SCM substitution blended systems.

Σ fᵢ (Cᵢ − C*):[I + P*(Cᵢ − C*)]⁻¹ = 0
Creep

Viscoelastic Homogenization

Extension to time domain via Laplace-Carson transform. Predicts basic creep compliance J(t,t₀) from C-S-H gel creep properties measured at the microscale.

J̃(s) = L{J(t)} → homogenize → J_eff(t)
Shrinkage

Eigenstress / Eshelby Model

Eshelby eigenstress formulation to predict autogenous and drying shrinkage from capillary pressure and pore microstructure. Linked to MIP-measured pore networks.

ε_shrink = −S : (C_eff)⁻¹ : Σ fᵢ Cᵢ : ε*ᵢ
Strength

Strength Upscaling

Nonlinear homogenization for predicting compressive and tensile strength from phase-level Drucker-Prager criteria. Validated on recycled aggregate systems and blended pastes.

f_c,eff = g(φ_CSH, H_nano, f_pore)
Multiphysics

Chemo-Mechanical Coupling

Coupled hydration-mechanics model tracking degree of hydration α(t), evolving phase assemblage, C-S-H packing density, and effective stiffness development over time.

C_eff(t) = f[α(t), η(t), V_phases(t)]

Phase-level Input Data · Real Measurement

Nanoindentation Grid Mapping & Statistical Deconvolution

Large-scale nanoindentation grids (up to several hundred indents per sample) on polished paste cross-sections. Statistical deconvolution identifies phase mechanical signatures: LD C-S-H, HD C-S-H, calcium hydroxide, unhydrated clinker, and SCM particles — feeding directly into homogenization models. The map on the right is built from an actual 10×10 indentation grid (100 indents, 60×60 µm field) measured by Oliver & Pharr analysis on a fresh cement paste sample.

From Published Research

Recycled Aggregate Micromechanics

Modeling recycled concrete aggregates as equivalent composite inclusions to capture the mechanical signature of the old attached mortar and old ITZ.

Recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) are heterogeneous by nature — a natural aggregate core surrounded by residual old mortar and a pre-existing interfacial transition zone (ITZ) inherited from the parent concrete. To account for this complexity in homogenization schemes, each RCA particle is represented as a multi-coated equivalent inclusion, replacing the true composite morphology with a homogeneous inclusion of equivalent stiffness — enabling direct integration into Mori-Tanaka / generalized self-consistent upscaling of recycled aggregate mortars and concretes.

📊 View Equivalent-Inclusion Figures & Morphology ⌄

Recycled aggregate replaced by a two-phase composite inclusion (natural aggregate core + old attached mortar), reduced to an equivalent homogeneous inclusion for use in analytical homogenization schemes.

Effective Shear Modulus Sensitivity

Normalized effective shear modulus of the equivalent inclusion as a function of the phase stiffness contrast E₀/E₁, for different old-mortar volume fractions f. The curves confirm that the equivalent-inclusion approximation converges toward the same asymptotic bounds regardless of morphology, validating its use for stiffness contrasts spanning several orders of magnitude.

📐 View Finite-Element Validation & Governing Equations ⌄

Axisymmetric finite-element mesh used to validate the analytical equivalent-inclusion scheme against full-field numerical simulations of the coated aggregate.

Interfacial Transition Zone

ITZ Characterization

The old ITZ inherited from the parent concrete — between the natural aggregate and the residual attached mortar — is systematically characterized by statistical nanoindentation grids, revealing a measurable stiffness gradient distinct from both the aggregate and the bulk cement paste.

🔬 View ITZ Characterization Figures ⌄

(a) Optical micrograph of the indentation region; (b) 2D indentation modulus map (0–180 µm); (c) corresponding 1D modulus profile M(GPa) across the granulat–ITZ–cement paste sequence at 28 days, showing a marked stiffness drop within the ~50 µm-wide ITZ before recovering to bulk paste values.

Principal Investigator

Dr. Ayodele
Adessina

Researcher in Civil Engineering at Cerema – Université Gustave Eiffel, specializing in the experimental and multiscale characterization of cementitious materials. My research bridges the gap between nanoscale C-S-H structure and macroscopic durability performance, with a particular focus on understanding the role of supplementary cementitious materials and recycled aggregates in shaping microstructure and long-term behavior.

Through micromechanical modeling and homogenization frameworks, I develop predictive tools for the mechanical and durability performance of low-carbon, sustainable cement-based systems.

Host Institution

UMR MCD — Materials for Sustainable Construction

Co-supervised research unit
Cerema — Université Gustave Eiffel

The UMR MCD (Matériaux pour une Construction Durable) is a joint research unit created on 28 February 2022, consolidating the former Cerema team DIMA (Durabilité, Innovation et valorisation des Matériaux Alternatifs) with the FM2D team (Formulation, Microstructure, Modélisation et Durabilité) of the Materials and Structures Department at Université Gustave Eiffel. The unit operates under the joint scientific supervision of both institutions, with sites in Aix-en-Provence and Sourdun (Cerema) and Marne-la-Vallée (Université Gustave Eiffel).

Its research addresses the durability of construction materials — cementitious and bituminous — for buildings and infrastructure, with a strong focus on integrating alternative and recycled materials (construction waste, industrial by-products) into a circular-economy perspective, reducing both resource depletion and environmental impact.

01
Interaction Mechanisms of Alternative Materials
Characterization, fresh-state and early-age formulation, evolution of physico-chemical and mechanical properties, and time-dependent modeling.
02
Durability in Service Environment
New ageing protocols, durability property assessment, predictive models, and validation on structural elements.
03
Life-Cycle & Circular Economy
Life-cycle inventory and assessment (LCI/LCA) of raw materials, processes, and final mix designs; environmental product declarations (FDES).

Mira de Béjaïa (Algeria), University of São Paulo (Brazil).
